utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I invite Mr. Kehoe to proceed, Mr. Leslie, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. If I could ask that P62 be brought up on the screen. General, there is the map that we have been talking about yesterday, and you mentioned during the course of your testimony about the artillery fire that you observed and you talked about the centre of town. With the assistance of the usher, could you please use the pen and mark with an X the area that you were referring to as the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have that -- a numbered placed on that and moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D118 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me go back and reference some of your testimony that you mentioned yesterday and you mentioned to us during the course of your testimony that shortly before Operation Storm tensions were mounting. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also mentioned for us -- and this would be on page 1939 at line 23, that the first confirmed indication we had - and you're talking about the attack - the first confirmed indication we had was roughly 20 minutes after 3.00 on the 4th when Sector South headquarters received an indication from UNCRO headquarters our superior headquarters in Zagreb, that an attack by the Croatian forces to capture the Krajina was imminent. You recall that, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to that, and going back to your comment that tensions were mounting, you were fully aware of fighting prior to that time going on between the HV and the Krajina Serbs in July of 1995, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also between the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can put up on the screen 65 ter 810. General, this is a document dated 28 July 1995, signed by the Supreme Defence Council of the Republic of Krajina, Serbian Krajina and on the 28th it notes that a state of war is declared on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? You were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen it prior to this occasion. I was aware of the documents being discussed by the time I was up at UNCRO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D119 admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, could you seek some clarification. The witness said: "I had not seen it prior to this occasion. I was aware of the documents being discussed by the time I was up at UNCRO headquarters," which both this occasion and the time when the witness was up at UNCRO headquarters is not immediately clear to me what date or what moment that refers to. Perhaps the witness could -- could you, Mr. Leslie, could you explain to me what you exactly meant there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To the best of my recollection, this is the first time that I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As well, to the best of my recollection, the knowledge that this document existed was being discussed and was a topic of conversation by the time I got to my new post as Chief of Staff UNCRO or at some period shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean just before or about the time of your arrival in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, my time in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Zagreb. Yes, because in Knin you were only -- you were Chief of Staff of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So General, is it your testimony that while you were in Sector South you had no knowledge that the army -- or the Republic of Serb Krajina had declared war on July 28th?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just a point of minor clarification. I would have raised previous occasion. Again in the interest of precision I think there is a distinction between declaring war and declaring a state of war, probably one that may not be significant for the immediate purpose but may be significant over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any distinction to be made Mr. Kehoe, then I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, I was not trying to parse words here. I will use any words in the document it was not a -- it was a distinction, frankly, that escaped me but I will use the word in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, is it your testimony that you were unaware that as of July 28th, 1995, the Republic of Serb Krajina had declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So are you saying that you were unaware or you knew?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware that such talk was out there, but until today I had not seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that the army of the -- army of the Republika Srpska in Bosnia and the army of the Serbian Krajina had joined forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, are you stating that as a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm asking the question: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware there were discussions and there was information that the three elements of the Serbian forces were cooperating very closely. I cannot recall if I was aware that they this actually joined force. I'm not sure what the context of joined forces means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were meetings -- let me withdraw that. Were you aware that Ratko Mladic had come to meet with the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina in Knin on 30 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will take your word for the date, but yes, sir, I was aware of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it have been -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're thinking of pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am thinking of pauses, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a good development. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, General, when you were the Chief of Staff in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was aware that such meetings were taking place prior to the outbreak of hostilities on the 4th. I can't specify as to when I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Now in -- you went on a patrol out of Knin on August the 3rd, and you saw an anti-tank organisation that you observed was very different from the other ARSK units that you had seen prior to that date, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was a unit that, for lack of a better term, was looked highly professional to you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It -- would you like me to elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on or about the 3rd of August. It was up towards the Livno valley. The soldiers were all in identical uniforms. The vehicles looked significantly newer than those that we were accustomed to seeing in Sector South on the side of the rebel Serbs and they were -- the aura of professionalism was markedly superior to the run of the mill of Serbian militia with whom we had some practice in dealing with in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about the vehicles that you observed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wheeled anti-tank guided missile systems. To the best of my recollection I only saw a couple, but it wasn't hard to figure out that there were more out there, but I have no direct knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you said this -- I'm sorry. You said, General, that this was in the Livno valley. Approximately how far from Knin was this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I could request a map, I could perhaps try and show you. It was -- I would hate to guess. It was some considerable distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not holding you to this General. Could you give us just a ballpark figure in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before one got up into the Livno valley. The terrain was highly canalizing. I would say very rough approximation somewhere between 15 to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was -- sorry. But this was still in the Republic of Serb Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you believed it at that time, General, that this was a unit from the Republika Srpska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, also on the 3rd, UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb sent Captain Williams down from Zagreb to consult with the headquarters in Sector South, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're stating that as a fact, sir, I will confer. I unfortunately don't recall when he showed up, but, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, you remember Captain Williams, a Canadian captain coming down from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But to be honest I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you remember that the reason he came down was to advise you and General Foran that a full attack would begin any day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the intelligence assessments of UNCRO headquarters G2 and UNPF that the possibility of an attack was climbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the information you were receiving was that it could happen as early as the next day, the 4th of August. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that part of the conversation if such ensued. But there were indications that an attack was imminent, I don't recall anybody actually specifying a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the indications that there was going to be an attack were coming from all quarters of the UN and I include Zagreb as well as New York, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to 1D170104 and it goes 0105.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can blow up that first page, Mr. Monkhouse. Is that correct? I don't believe this is the correct document. Your Honour, I think I called up the wrong page. If I can pull up -- 1D170102. Now, this is a -- if we can blow up that page. This is an outgoing cable from Kofi Annan to Mr. Akashi in Zagreb, dated 3rd of August 1995. If we can turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can just read some of this briefly. As discussed this afternoon, and by the way this it likewise dated the 3rd of August, 1995 when we scroll down we'll be able to see that. Scroll back up, please. "As discussed this afternoon, the prospects for war in Croatia continue to appear alarmingly high despite the significant concessions announced by the Croatian Serbs in Geneva. The security of the United Nations personnel in this situation is therefore of major concern, both in UNPF and here at headquarters. Ambassador Albright plans to call you this afternoon to express her government's conviction that we are not doing enough in this regard." Go to the second sentence in the next paragraph. I won't read all of this, beginning with however: "However there is no escaping the basic reality that the overwhelming majority of UNCRO personnel is deployed in Serbian-controlled [Realtime transcript read in error "certain-controlled"] territories. They are located in observation posts, at border crossings and check-points. Their barracks, offices, and residences are all in Serb-ruled towns. Whether in small groups or large, they are all vulnerable to attack or capture." If I can go to the first sentence in the next -- the last paragraph, beginning with: "Ambassador Albright." Ambassador Albright has made clear that her government's view that the continued presence of United Nations personnel in exposed conditions reveals, "ineptitude, on our part and that our vulnerability, reduces the options of the international community."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I was listening to the French but I wondered whether page 9, line 15 reflect what you said. The certain controlled territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be Serb-controlled territories, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was there in French so I thought it would be what you said in English. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as of the 3 August, General, there was deep, deep concern in the United Nations about the safety of UN personnel that were living in Serb towns, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in fact, you note that Ambassador Albright described leaving those people out in Serb-held areas and living in Serb-held areas was inept, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note her opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could even read it, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the 3rd. Now, you noted for us you were getting information coming from Zagreb about the growing tensions, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on the day of the 3rd, the day before Storm, that was supposed to be your last day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on the evening of the 3rd, you along with other members of the UN contingent were downtown having a going away dinner, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if it was on the 2nd or the 3rd. But if you have people who say it was on the 3rd, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is true. You were having a going away dinner down there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On either the 2nd or the 3rd. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now during that dinner and Grace Kang was there, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Grace Kang was an UN employee, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during the course of this dinner, you and Ms. Kang spoke to Ambassador Galbraith on the telephone. And he told to you go to the compound didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a conversation between himself and the lady in question. At some point she turned the phone over to me and quite frankly I did not understand his point. He was saying, Are our positions secure? And I said, What are you trying to tell us Mr. Ambassador have you informed UNCRO headquarters and by the way I'm certainly not going to ask my area commander to initiate the sirens that night which may trigger a whole sequence of events, and the conversation stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me very clear, is it your testimony that Ambassador Galbraith did not advise you during that conversation to go to the compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall no such conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the Canadian ambassador to Croatia at that time was a Mr. Graham Green, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Green, Ambassador Green, likewise advised the Canadian contingent in the evening hours of 3 August 1995 that an attack was going come the next morning. Didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you remember Captain Belarose [phoen], don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know that he advised the Tribunal that at 11.00, 2300 hours on 3 August, he spoke to you and the Operations Officer Duso [phoen] who told him that an attack was going to occur on the morning of the 4th. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that that was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have that conversation with Captain Belarose?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there were many conversations on the evenings, several of them from the 1st of August, onwards as to what the probability of the attack by the Croats into the rebel Serb enclave of the Krajina as to when it might occur. There may well have been multiple conversations with individuals that you mention, all of it speculative in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So warnings coming from New York, warnings coming from Zagreb, warnings potentially coming from the ambassador of the United States, warnings potentially coming from the ambassador, the Canadian ambassador, to Croatia, plus information in the OPs officer that was not sufficient for you, Colonel, to conclude that an attack was going to take place the next day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there were also warnings from Croatian military authorities. There were warnings from Serbian military authorities. There was warnings from the local population. The indicators were climbing as were the tensions, but as to the exact moment or even day of the attack, the first confirmed indication we got was via the military chain of command from UNCRO headquarters into our operations centre at approximately 0320 hours on the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, in your previous question you took all the warnings that you have put to the witness before, as warnings that reached him the testimony was that certainly not all of them reached them so therefore it is improper that all the warnings did not lead him because that suggests and does not fully reflect the testimony of the witness that all these warnings reached him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you please refrain from including such suggestions in this way in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a fact -- well, there was a Canadian battalion in the zone of separation, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were in contact with that Canadian battalion, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Foran's command team, which I was a member, was in contact with all the battalions, including the Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, they were informed at 2200 hours on the 3rd of August that an attack was going to ensue the following morning, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, sir, and I don't have any such documentation in front of me, they were informed that the risks were high for an attack sometime in the immediate future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The risks were high. Sir, you were -- well, do you recall -- you testified yesterday that the UN sector security person was Andries Dreyer. Do you remember you said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now Andries Dreyer told this Court last week that the person responsible from taking a condition from code orange to code red was you, and I will give you the page reference; 1754 at line 24, beginning in 16: "How made the decision? I apologise. Who made the decision as to when the alert level was going to go from orange to red? Answer: The decision on the alert levels at that point in time was in the hands of the military. Question: And who in the military? Answer: In the military within our compound it rested with the Chief of Staff. Question: And who was that. The Chief of Staff at that time was Colonel Leslie." Now you were the person who was going make the decision as to whether or not this was going to move from a code orange to a code red, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you are at headquarters at Sector South at 11.00 in the evening when you had a discussion with Belarose and Duso about an attack coming the next morning, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed often the potential of an attack. Let me, if you will permit, point out some issues that may be related to where I believe you intend to go with your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, just answer the question. You can go back on redirect and give a speech. Please, I just want to you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Kehoe, it's not totally ununderstandable that the witness responds in this way. I agree with you that the witness doesn't have to bother about your line of questioning. Nevertheless, you repeat questions sometimes where you apparently are not very happy with the answers and that of course makes people think of lines of questions where you are heading for and quite honest it came into my mind a couple of times as well. Please put your question and if you would please answer them and we will keep a close eye on whether the questions are repetitious or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I was responsible to my commander for the security status of Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when I asked you before about Mr. Dryers' statement that you as Chief of Staff was the person that made the decision whether this was going to move from a code orange to a code red, the answer to that, is, yes, it is you, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely, sir, because there were implications of moving to code red in Sector South headquarters not of least of which was initiating emergency recall, hitting the air-raid sirens and triggering a variety of the responses throughout the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you had -- I'm sorry. If you had triggered the air-raid sirens and you had gone to a code red General, you wouldn't have had security personnel out at 5.00 in the morning in soft skinned vehicles picking up civilians would you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Leslie is a witness here not a person who has to answer to, well, let's say questions which come close to accusations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, as a result of not going to a code red at 11.00 in the morning -- excuse me, 11.00 in the evening on the 3rd of August, UN personnel and Mr. Dryer at 5.00 in the morning were forced to go out in soft skin vehicles and begin the retrieval of UN personnel who were living in the town. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to answer this question because the question is put in such a way that it puts an monocausal situation to you and where Mr. Kehoe does not accept that you explain and try to elaborate on what you really find. Mr. Kehoe, if I say that -- well, you are putting matters in a monocausal situation. If you say, did this contribute, usually we have things are not as simple as they look at first sight. What kind of vehicles do you have; what information reached you; what -- if you would ask the witness whether the fact that did he not -- that if he would have decided that code red would apply, that the situation might have been different, fine. It is a factor in a cause of events. And that's how the chamber would look at matters and not as isn't it true that this is the result of that. Hardly a situation is the result of one other factor, but usually of a complex of factors. Would you keep that in mind and please condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course you would ask the witness if he ask it in a different way whether that would change the situation. That's perfectly right, but if you put it as a monocausal question to him he doesn't have to respond to that. If you want to the extent -- Mr. Kehoe allows you to explain what you mean, of course can you do it, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, some of the discussions which took place the night of the 3rd and the night of the 1st and the 2nd because there were a variety of opinions and rumour and conversations from a variety of sources saying that attack was imminent, was that in the absence of a relatively definitive opinion and asteer from our chain of command, the possibility of initiating emergency recall procedures in Knin, the capital of the rebel Serbs might well have triggered a precipitous assault either one way or another across the entirety of the Krajina we had to be synchronised with our fellow sector, Sector East, Sector North, Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just waiting for the translator to finish, Judge, I can see in the booth that she is still translating. Sir, your highest responsibility was the safety of UN personnel, safety and security of UN staff, want it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our highest responsibility was to fulfil our mission as dictated by the United Nations security council resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And part of that responsibility, the high responsibility was the safety and security of UN staff.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, safety and security of UN staff and soldiers is a prime and critical concern but it does not mitigate against meeting our mission imperatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't go on red alert according to your direct examination until 3.20 in the morning, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm just, I'm sorry, I don't exactly have a copy of transcript here, so I can't see when they've finished. I've got it now, sir. Thank you. Just to be clear, sir, I received from the OP centre at roughly 3.20 shortly after that, General Foran and I discussed the issue, so I can't give a precise time when we actually hit or went to what you call code red which involved hitting the air-raid sirens and a variety of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to mix with the nomenclature code red alert or red alert or a red level. What is the proper description?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Low state red.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Low state red. Now, when you -- given the information that you had on the evening of the 3rd, where you didn't go to the alert level red, you didn't do that, because you did not expect the HV, the Croatian army, to attack the centre of gravity, did you, Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think you're making an assumption that the centre of gravity was Knin. There is a professional debate as to the validity of that comment, or we could certainly have one. And I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it was in fact the capital of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely sir. Having said that, the centre of gravity is that one single item which will either you must defend or attack respectively between the enemy and the Defence, and in the case, and I believe you have already referred to it, the centre of gravity arguably for the rebel Serbs was the connection to the Serbs in Bosnia and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the location where they had their Ministry of Defence, their parliament, their President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's try first to see what we can learn as far as facts are concerned. That's of course the difficulty if you put a composite question that you suggest to the witness that he did not believe that the HV would attack Knin, and then you added the centre of gravity. Let's first try to find out whether the witness believed that the HV would attack Knin and let's leave aside for a second whether that was the centre of gravity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, we believed that the HV would attack Knin but didn't have a high degree of certainty that it would occur on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So timing -- you had doubt on the timing so soon but not that the HV would attack Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You believed at that time, didn't you, that any attack that came from the HV was going to come in a traditional fashion from the east, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when the attack in fact took place, and this goes back to the statement that you made in 2003 that's in D116, you noted they pulled off the attack with a degree of expertise. You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you did not think on the evening of the 3rd that the HV had that expertise, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't recall what I thought at that time on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if you thought -- if you made a judgment that they had that expertise, might you have acted differently?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if you knew that they had the expertise that they demonstrated on the 4th of August, that would not have given you reason to go to code red?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if I understand the context of your question, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, sir, you misjudged what the situation was, on the evening of the 3rd, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 3rd there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you didn't, in conjunction with General Foran, declare a code red and bring the UN personnel into the compound, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that we didn't declare a code red on the evening of the 3rd and bring the UN personnel into the compound at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if you knew that the attack was going to take place at 5.00 a.m. on the 4th of August, would you have declared a code red in the evening hours of the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is speculative. Probably. But, once again, I would probably have to certainly discuss that with the other folk who were there to see what our thinking was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to clarify this one answer, Your Honour, and I don't want to repeat anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony General that if you knew an attack was going to take place on the 4th of August at 5.00 p.m. [sic] as we sit here it is speculative whether or not would you have declared a code red?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what the witness said and you are really repeating your question, he said speculative to the extent, he could also say hypothetical, and if you are answering a hypothetical question that leads you almost always to speculation because he has testified now five times he didn't know that, he didn't expect that to happen on the next morning. He expected this to happen somewhere in the near future and I must say the more I listen to you it is clear, that you consider that this witness should have acted in a different way on the basis of the knowledge he had. He has now explained to us what his knowledge was. He explained what he did. And apparently you're -- you really think that he should have acted differently. That is perfectly clear to the Chamber now. So would you please come to the point for all of this, then we'd like to hear that. If not, would you please move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I might make a matter to the transcript on line 24, it notes that in the page 20, it is correct that we did declare and I think he missed -- General Leslie said, "we did not declare." I believe the negative is missing from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge, line 24, page 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is it correct that we did not declare a code red on the evening of the 3rd. Yes, that is perfectly clear that it is not correct in the transcript at this moment and will be corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us move, if we can to the events of the 4th. Now, you noted for us that you were in a bunker and I believe this testimony is at -- if I may. Page 1944, lines 21 through 25. You noted that and I'm talking about line 21: "From the moment of the initial barrage number approximately 6.00, I do not recall having any time to actually watch where the shell fire was landing." So, at least during that period of time, you don't have any idea where these shells were going in Knin, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not. One minor correction. I was not in a bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. I think you had said you were walking around the compound. But the point being that up until approximately 6.00 you didn't know where the point these things were impacting, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So from 5.00 to 6.00 you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6.00 is an approximate time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after 6.00, and if we can turn to -- and this is from P84. And if we can go to page 2 of this document. I'm sorry, it is again, Your Honour this is the -- page 2, paragraph 2, because the sequence of numbers is a little off. Now, that top paragraph, and if we can start with the line: "However," it is about one, two, three ... about ten lines down. If we can blow that up just a bit. Now, about ten lines -- actually it is about eight lines down, you said: "However, at about 6.00 Bravo, I returned to my office to get back to work and during breaks and speaking on the telephone or radio, went out to the balcony of the third floor to observe the shell fire." Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is also the time-frame that you told us that you got into, had gone down to the front gate and had got into an APC to travel into Knin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is all in the 6.00 time-frame, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Somewhere between before 6.00 and somewhere before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you continue on here, you say: "The salvos of fire appear to be by batteries of between four and six guns with most of the fire grouped around the centre of town." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I wrote it and it was relatively fresh in my mind, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in the 6.00 hour, most of the fire was directed towards the -- the centre of town, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this time-frame, sir, in addition to you talking on the telephone, taking care of other personnel, making sure people were safe, you were talking to the media as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a very short period of time. But I think the main conversations with the media happened at around 6.45 or 7.00, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 6.45. Let's go to 1D170386. Now, before we go to this particular item, if we can. Who did you speak to, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in what context?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who from the media were you speaking to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was it multiple news agencies?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, during the course of the 4th, you did in fact talk to multiple media sources, both TV and print, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some points during the day, yes, but how many and in what context and what time, I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us go to this particular tape and this is a BBC tape and as we see it is 7.04 on the morning of the 4th, London time which of course would be 8.00 a.m. Zagreb/Knin time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we could play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Short time ago we spoke to the UNPROFOR spokesman in Knin, Lieutenant Colonel Andrew Leslie, he described how the offensive there began. "At 0500 this morning, Knin, the capital of the Krajina was hit by artillery and rocket shells. It was dark at that time, of course, the center or the main point of impact appeared to be the center of Knin, after 300 detonations we've lost count. Reports from our battalions indicate that essentially every large urban center in the Krajina has been hit by shell fire, starting between 5 and 5.30. As well the Croats have launched their strikes on the town of Gracac. There's a lot of shell fire. There has not been yet a lot of movement into the zone, so we don't really have a clear picture on what the Croatian ground forces are doing now but they certainly pounded the Serbian communities "There's two or three pillars of fire and smoke in the centre of Knin. We unfortunately had some of our people still sleeping downtown when this happened and ... civilians mostly, and we sent our armoured vehicles to collect them. The term controlled "chaos," from our view, applies. The damage? It is very hard to assess, I mean, there's houses that are destroyed, there's craters in the roads, it is not terribly pleasant."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, that interview is talking about what has been going on over the recent hour since the attack took place, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you note in here that the mean point of impact was the centre of town. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't say -- and again, and there is it encompassing both the 6.00 time-frame that you observed as well as the 7.00 to 8.00 time-frame, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to clarify that a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The interview took place approximately 8.00 a.m. Knin time, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I think so. If you say it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you are describing events that took place between -- what you observed between 5.00 a.m. and approximately 8.00 a.m., aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you are describing the -- where the shells were falling, you say the mean point of impact is the centre of town. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't ever describe it as something that there were shells falling all over the place. Did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not describe it as shells falling all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your memo that you wrote days later, P84, you also don't describe that the shells were falling all over the place, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this time-frame, sir -- and by the way, as we talk about this, and reading the transcript. You went out on this one trip, is that right, where you -- with these Jordanian to get some CIVPOL people and some people jumped in the back and nothing significant happened, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you received a medal didn't you for participating in rescuing 40 UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the Meritorious Service Medal for meritorious performance for my performance as Chief of Staff both in Sector South and UNCRO. Meritorious service medals are not awarded for acts of bravery, curage, or distinction, therefore a job done well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that -- the next step that you are going to access whether it was granted to this witness or not. Are there any other matters you would like to deal with which are so far away from what this case is really about, it is not about who gets medals for what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can talk to you outside the presence of the witness of exactly what my basis of is for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is anything then please come to your point quickly, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will before the next break, I will talk to Your Honour outside the presence of the witness exactly where I'm going with that. I will postpone the questions until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the day, General, on the 4th, you were in steady contact with your headquarters in Zagreb, didn't you ?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not. The operations centre was in steady contact with Zagreb. My remit, because General Foran had excellent command and control because he was located in the OP centre my remit was to essentially just take care of things in the headquarters location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when the calls were coming back from Zagreb were you discussing them with anyone such as General Foran and others?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When calls went into the operation centre if I was around, then, yes, I would be brought into the loop. Every time I swung by the headquarters building I would drop there and get an OPs update but I was not personally in constant contact with Zagreb, which was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you went past the operations centre and were talking to people who were in communication with Zagreb, were questions being asked from Zagreb as to why Sector South had not declared a code red the night before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they asking questions, why had UN personnel were still out in the Knin community and not in the compound at the time the attack ensued?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, they were being told, were they not, at the level of shelling, that was transpiring, were they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that a variety of operations updates were sent with a high degree of frequency as to what we taught was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were informing Zagreb, were you also talking to various media sources and describing to them the level of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, as were many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the same time -- by the way, who were the others that were informing media sources that -- about the shelling, besides you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier General Foran and Mr. Alan Roberts, I believe, who was the sector information officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now during this same period of time General this is the period of time when the protest letter is drafted, the morning of the 4th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring this up, P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now General this is the letter that the Prosecution put into evidence as P83, the letter that was supposed to go to General Gotovina. Did you read this letter before it went out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that such a letter was going to be sent. I do not recall reading it before it went out, as I believe you can see by the nomenclature was drafted by the senior liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This letter, was it sent to UNCRO headquarters on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it sent to media sources on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you were talking to the media sources about what happened on the 4th, did you tell these media sources that 1500 shells had fallen on Knin during the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have. I can't recall, but I'm -- I might well have. That number seems to resinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you tell them that on the 5th, another 1500 shells had fallen on Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I was precise. I think I said approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, didn't you say that it was a conservative estimate, sir, that 500 shells and I can direct to you your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I understand what I said and when I said it. But I think it is an approximate figure and not an absolute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, you said that in your statements in 1996, 1997 several times, 1998, you repeated the conservative estimate of 3.000 shells, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is what you were telling Zagreb right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is what you were telling the media?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor several weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the course of that statement, you told the Prosecutor that these were not personal estimates, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And so the number of projectiles that you told the media and Zagreb and other sources, wasn't correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, these are approximate numbers. I cannot attest to 2099 or 3001 shells landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, General, how many projectiles actually fell?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have an approximation, sir. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, based on what you were -- by the way, before we even move to that, were you telling, were you telling the media sources as well as Zagreb that there were many, many people that died as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you tell them, sir, if I may, that -- and this is on the 1996 statement, page number 00527691, the death estimates of 300 to 500 personnel -- excuse me. A conservative estimate of the number of artillery shells fired at Knin over four and five is 3.000. The result is about 300 houses being damaged? You don't know that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no -- I did not see the house -- I did not see 300 houses being damaged. It is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't see -- but you were telling the media in Zagreb that 300 houses were being damaged?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. This is moving fairly quickly and sometime this is happens we're going from a reference in a statement back to generic references to discusses with the media at various times and I think the witness needs to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we're referring to. Mr. Kehoe, first of all, that -- the report which is now in evidence already shows that figures used by this witness at first sight appear not to be always very precise. If I just draw your attention to the fact that he say during the first two hours, 300 projectiles were fired and then the next line is that the rate of impact diminished to about one round every few seconds. Now 300 rounds in two hours is on round every 24 seconds so to say that is reduced by one round every few seconds unless you consider a few seconds more than 24 seconds, that already demonstrates that there seems to be a type of accuracy which would need further explanation if he would rely on that. I do agree with Mr. Tieger, that if we put to the witness that he said something to the media, then of course the Chamber would have to know what he actually said to the media to see whether this question is fair. At the same time, this Chamber is not blind and not deaf for what was said to the media at that time. But at the same time our primary focus should be on what happened and that giving information to the media plays a role is not ignored, but let try to keep everything in balance, that is that we first of all are interested in what happened, and to the extent that what was said to the media adds something to that knowledge or can tell us about wrong impression given by mistake or on purpose, that's all well understood, and therefore I'm not saying that it is irrelevant but we should try to keep the balance between what we are looking at and first of all what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge, and if I just have some latitude I think you will understand where I'm going in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it you're going in some direction, but you're not going very quickly, it appears to us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to the rate of fire that Judge Orie just referred to, in your statement of 12 August 1995, if we might clear that up, you told the Prosecution for the first time several weeks ago that that rate of fire should not have been taken literally, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to some of the items that you were talking to at the time --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, may I refer to a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do we have copies? All of them ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you also tell the people in Zagreb that as a result of the shelling that three to 500 personnel of which the vast majority were civilians predominantly women, children, and elderly were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked for a casualty estimate. Yes, we gave them an estimate in that range of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And upon what did you base that information that you gave to Zagreb after the shelling on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on discussions amongst the staff. Based on what they were interacting with a variety or the information they were gleaning from a variety of the close to 1.000 Serbian displaced persons who had ended up in our compound on the evening of the 4th. And it was -- it was estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, had anybody done any investigation whatsoever to make a determination as of 5 August 1995 that three to 500 people had been killed as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, we were locked inside our camp and were unable to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Locked inside your camp, sir. You went to the hospital on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was prior to the Croatians actually getting to the front gate of Sector South. From the moment they arrived we were unable to leave as I think has been clearly shown in a variety of news cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, it's a fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to Exhibit D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a statement from Mr. Carl Bildt at the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, if I may, talking about the attack and it notes in the second page -- excuse me, the third paragraph: "This" talking about the attack, "it will cast a dark shadow over Croatia for a long time to come. Especially appalling is the shelling of the civilian population now being reported." Now those reports of the civilian population being shelled were coming from you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one source amongst many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were the one source, the other source that it was coming from were individuals in the Sector South compound, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you recall -- if you're referring to "you" as the collective of personnel in Sector South compound, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This, sir, was being imparted to UN headquarters based on no investigate at all, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems to me the issue of investigate dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you first asked on what basis this witness gave his assessments and you asked whether there had been any investigations and this gives the context I think of what happened here, that there were no formal investigations nothing let's investigate this or that but that information was gathered. That is at least what I learned from your evidence in this respect until now. Is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start analysing statements of all kinds of other persons, are you aware of all the sources Mr. Bildt had available before you gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we move through the 4th there was still fighting taking place in and around Knin between the ARSK and the HV, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there was no fighting taking place in Knin on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There were a lot of Serb soldiers in Knin weren't there on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it is definition when you say fighting that shelling or is that direct combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me re-ask my question and we'll start again. Were there Serb soldiers in Knin throughout the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there Serb soldiers moving through Knin throughout the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there fighting still going on in the surrounding hills in -- in and around Knin in the evening hours of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the ARSK and the HV were fighting well, into the night of the 4th, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct visual observation of such, but the reports that we were getting from our battalions in the zone of separation and from others, the UNMOs, would support that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a late evening clip from BBC on the 8th that you gave at 20 minutes to 11.00. Sorry, on the 4th of August of 1995. And if I may this is again BBC beginning at 2340 on the 4th of August. And it is 1D170387.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "REPORTER: We're joined now on the telephone by Colonel Andrew Leslie who is in command of the UN detachment in Knin. Colonel Leslie is the assault continuing, or has it gone quiet for the night? "LESLIE: It is continuing but at a reduces tempo. It's still the occasional shell landing in Knin. We still have reports of fire-fighting all up and down the line, but I think there has been a built of a pause while people are trying to sort themselves out, replenish and deal with their casualties. "REPORTER: In your judgment, are the Croats on the point of taking the town. "LESLIE: Taking Knin? No. We've had no reports of Croatians being within direct fire range of Knin and there's still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills so ... there we go."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, as of 2340 Knin time, it was your conclusion that Knin was not about to fall to the HV, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's what I said exactly. Whatever words I used at that time are the words that I felt to be true. I don't think I used quite those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's play it back?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to get it as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I'm just waiting for it to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm waiting for it to be played. Who made it play last time? Would he please repeat what he or she did at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think the transcript is locked too. Maybe it would be a good time for a break and we can correct this and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way of scrolling through the transcript of what was just said so that -- oh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour I think I can read the transcript. I do have the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is again at page 36, lines -- he keeps moving it. At lines?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir for what it is worth. Line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question comes from the reporter, can you just scroll down. The question comes from the reporter. In your judgment are the Croats on the point of taking the town? And you respond: "Taking Knin? No, we have had no reports of Croatians being within direct fire range of Knin and there's still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills, so there we go." My question to you was: As of 2340, almost midnight on the night of the 4th, it was your conclusion or position that Knin was not about to fall to the HV. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that specific point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this transcript, you used the term Serbs and I think you say there are a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills. When you say "Serbs" you're talking about Serb soldiers, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to put myself back in that time and I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you are talking about civilians would there and we are talking about direct fire range, because the question -- your answer is taking Knin, No, we have no reports of Croatians being in direct fire range of Knin. Now in Croatians there, you are talking about the HV soldiers, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And logically, as you begin, Croatian being in direct fire range of Knin there are still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills. Logically the word Serbs there being in the surrounding hills you're talking about Serb soldiers, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, sir, I can't recall to the frame of mind to what I said. Serbs is Serbs and I don't make any distinction between civilians and military in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't make any differences between military and civilian, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the context of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you do make the distinction when talking about Croats you're talking about soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think back to what I was thinking 12 years ago on a media interview at midnight. It is really tough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to another topic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps take a longer pause that you usually do, Mr. Kehoe, that is a pause for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I move this now this particular exhibit, or shall I wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you played two portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, Judge, I think we have three to move it so we can move this at the beginning of the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we going to deal with them all as one. Mr. Registrar I see you're nodding, no, you prefer to have them all separate. Then Mr. Tieger is there any objections against the ones we've seen until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the exhibits. Apart from the videos there is still the outgoing cable, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Registrar, could you already assign a number to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, the document which was the outgoing cable by and now I ... Mr. Registrar, or Mr. Kehoe perhaps you could help us -- assigned by Mr. Bildt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, the first is a outgoing cable from Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi dated 3 August, it is a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has not yet received a number. Any objection Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar that would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D121 has been admitted into evidence. And then the next one I think is the Bildt document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was in. Then we have then the two videos. The first one, both videos, 4th of August. One in the morning hours at in the morning hours and the other one in the late evening hours. The first one, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the sake of clarity this is the video numbered 1D170386 and this becomes D122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D122 is admitted into evidence, then we have the second video-clip, Mr. Registrar that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document ID 1D170387 and it becomes D123.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D123 is admitted into evidence. We resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked to start without the presence of the witness. The Chamber was briefed about a conversation that has taken place during the break between you, Mr. Kehoe, and you, Mr. Tieger, as to the reasons to put further questions for the -- for the reasons for which the witness received a medal. That is -- so we have superficial knowledge of which direction you would like to go in that respect. There is, as such, no problem, if you want to go in that direction. But this is an general observation. That is, do everything that you do in approximately a third of the time you take for it. It is not very efficient what you are doing and it might be that sometimes you expect a trier of fact not to catch the issue quickly and that would you have to go over the same ground for a couple of times and that is really not necessary. I just want to tell you that. And therefore, no problem to deal with the matter but try to do it really as efficiently as possible, come to the point right away, no ritual bounces as I often say. Let's get to the point right away and let's also not forget that this case is not about mistakes or things witnesses have done wrong in the past. Of course, if there are any issues that shed additional light on reliability or credibility of course you can deal with the matter, but the core of this case is that this chamber hears evidence about what happened at that time, and of course also that the Chamber receives relevant information which assists us in assessing credibility and reliability, but try to find a balance and do it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Leslie. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, directing your attention to the 5th of August, the fighting between the HV and the ARSK continued in the 5th of August as well, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted that soldiers and military equipment were moving through Knin on the 5th, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to recall if there was actual soldiers and military equipment moving through Knin on the 5th and the answer is yes, in the very early hours of the morning. I did not see any soldiers or equipment certainly when I was downtown at approximately 9.00 in the morning of the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there was a tank in front of your compound returning -- an ARSK tank in front of the UN compound that was returning fire on the 5th, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to 1D170076.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a second edition Toronto Star article. If we can just scroll up a bit. And I think we're talking about the third paragraph. You noted that the Croats have very close. Serb tanks are returning fire right outside our compound and artillery is impacting inside Knin. Residents are gone." Now, the Serb tanks that you are referring to, of course, are ARSK tanks aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears to be a newspaper article in which there appears to be a quote. Let's first ask the witness whether this is what he said and then we'll ask him what he meant. Yes. Is this you're quoted here in apparently a -- I can't see it was on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Toronto --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Toronto, yes. Is this -- are you correctly quoted here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you imagine that you have given such a statement to the press, looking at the content.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can imagine something similar to this, but I do not recall a Serb tank ever being right outside our compound. I do not recall saying that. I have no memory of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me also, Mr. Kehoe, look at your first question. ARSK tank in front of the compound. It was returning fire ... Yes, could we move on a little bit so that we see the -- what appears above "body." Yes. Yes, I'm trying to understand, Mr. Kehoe, where I find a reference to the date. Apart from the date of the newspaper, but I'm just trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you look in this, Your Honour, it says the Croats are very close. Serb tanks are returning fire right outside our compound and artillery is impacting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Early this morning. It says early this morning from Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Early this morning. Yes, that means that we are talking about early this morning. Yes. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I won't belabour this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, but you don't recall this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have this marked and received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, earlier the registry mistakenly skipped number D120. Therefore, this document will become D120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D120 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, General, to 65 ter 4696. And, General, if we can move to page 3 of that document. Now, General, if we can just and tell me if you page your way through, this is an UNMO report from the 5th of August. And on the third page under -- excuse me, page 4. I'm sorry, I have been corrected. It is page 4. And we're talking about CanBat and the UNMO team Gracac, so if can we just move that up a bit. Now, it notes in this document there are any number of targets. And did you get information on the 5th that these pieces of equipment were moving towards Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall doing so. I'm looking at the time, and if you'll forgive me sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take your time, sir.
