utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just see when this was sent or, more importantly received at UNCRO headquarters. So if you just go back up to the top, you should have a date, time group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can read to you General on the first page. On the 5th, it is 1900 Bravo.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is on the 5th in the evening. That's illogical, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can go to the front page, sir. If you want to go to the front page you can check the time and date.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hostilities were over on the 5th so to have Serbian forces moving through Knin at 1900 hours on the 5th is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can he with go to the actual time sequence under CanBat and if we can go back to page 4, I can give you a more direct time as to when this was observed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4. Now it notes in the first sequence that this was reported apparently at 0535, that's the first observation, of some tanks and other mechanised -- pieces of mechanised equipment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if you look down I think you will see that the next item is at 0530, as we move towards the bottom of that page, there's another one from 0550, and you see the item towards the third -- the second-to-last line that the heading towards Knin. If we turn to the next page, Mr. Registrar, and if I'm going too fast?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it is quite already. May I interject occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you specify whether equipment is Serbian or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe that the inset at the beginning is ARSK, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go back to the CanBat line, if we go back one page. On the CanBat report, I believe he is talking about RSK items, you see that on the line?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the first line, agreed. The subsequent ones I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page are we now on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We are now on page 5. You are on page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's 84, last two digits of the ERN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 85, yes, which is the fifth page of this document, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir I have the document. I stand ready for the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these documents reflect a report, a reporting that is equipment moving towards Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my question to you is were you aware, if you know that the RSK was moving equipment of this magnitude if it is from RSK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Obviously my concern was building into the question that the equipment was RSK. Now I think Mr. Kehoe amended that to indicate a conditional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thinks are going a bit too quickly for me at this moment. We earlier turned to page 4 and you were referring to the first line of the CanBat portion of the document as a demonstration that it was RSK rather than anything else. Now let me try to understand what this paragraph 3 CanBat 1 report, how it is structured. It says: "CanBat 1," reported, and then we get several elements of the report the ARSK reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. But I don't have the hard copy of this I'm trying to follow on screen and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I. You know that in e- court you can get your own copy and move it as you wish. That's what I'm doing at this moment. The reference to RSK is within the first part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore your suggestion is that what follows in the other elements of the report would be covered by this reference to RSK. That's at least how I understood your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it is not the only reference and what I taking the General to was yet the next page, the page that -- and it does have several references to ARSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go down do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever there is a reference to in a specific portion then it is clear that this portion refers to a certain armed force. If there's not, then the question first should be put, What armed forces or equipment of what armed forces we are talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we just move down a bit on that other page, General, and I'm looking at an entry again with CanBat reporting on the 5th at 1300 near Kistanje, en route towards Knin. Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have Croatian shelling Canadian OPs on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see the entry, sir, at 1300 right there. Is that here? Should be?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that page we are talking about, if we may, again 1300 at 05 near Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] CanBat reporter ARSK --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not found it yet. Could you please guide me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Do you see where it says 1 Sagger and just go up three lines at it says at approximate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge, there is no neat way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said earlier that we catch certain issue very quickly. I am now demonstrating that we sometimes do not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So my comment would this occurred at 1300 hours on the 5th. It is highly unlikely that these ARSK weapons systems were in Knin because I can attest -- I was there that the Croatian was right in Knin and certainly at our front gate before 100 hours and the route from Kistanje down must inevitably go by the front gate of the camp. So my conclusion without knowing full details is that those weapons systems never made it into the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just take you to one item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- try to understand, we are approximate time is given near, Kistanje en-route towards Knin, CanBat report, ARSK is a reference to the armed force, 325 I take it that's the number and then T-34, T-35 sounds to me as these would be tanks. Is that correctly understood? And then again three to five, T-54, 55, which sounds as tanks to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then five times six M55 three X, five times a six MS -- M55 stands for? I'm just trying to understand what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was going to you know follow up with the, Judge -- with the General and ask what type equipment generally we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know that was still to follow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General and I understand this is the first time you have seen this document, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I have seen it before, I cannot recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fair enough. Give us an idea and the Chamber an idea, if you could, based on your expertise what type of equipment we're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to restrict comments to the subparagraph or the contact was reported at 1300 on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be a good place to start, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understood, so this is a Canadian observation post sending radio message and text messages to Sector South headquarters and informing the UNMO chain that they have identified as of 1.00 on the 5th, five medium battle tanks, T-34/35, three or five slightly larger bigger tanks, five self-propelled systems. Sagger refers to a anti-tank guided missile system. A BRDM is essentially a four-wheeled armoured car of which two of these have an anti-tank system traditionally mounted on their top. And three to five CP vehicles -- CP is the more or less accepted military abbreviation for command post. Two times ten-tonne trucks with trailers is self-explanatory. Two to three T-12s. T-12s are an anti-tank gun; very long barrel, very low. And 12 APC; APC refers to armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is one entry. This does indicate to you, General, that the ARSK had weapons in the area at least in the afternoon of the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it indicates that where these things were reported those weapons systems were but it does not to my mind that they were in or in very close proximity to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier invited you, Mr. Kehoe, to be very clear on what bullet points a reference to ARSK is appearing. You have read this now, Mr. Leslie. I see that the time reference at approximately 1300 hours that then a reference is made to ARSK equipment and then we see a new bullet point where the Sagger starts is that still since there is no new time is that the time and would be included in the information in the bullet point just above that, or how do you interpret that? I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I would suggesting it is the former. In other words, as Defence counsel is claiming, I agree with him, the way it is currently crafted. The ARSK at sub-bullet 0513 Bravo, then you have ARSK 3- everything after that up until the next time block is probably the Canadians referring to ARSK equipment and personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same armed forces and same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you and D124 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the General in charge of the RSK was General Mrksic, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he in fact didn't leave Knin until the morning of the 5th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know. There -- I didn't know at the time and there are varying opinions - that's all they are, opinions, that flowed back and forth between those who were closely involved in the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the Office of the Prosecutor in the 16th of July of 1998 that General Mrksic took commander of the ARSK in mid-July until he fled on the morning of the 5th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I was not speaking from a point of view of personal fact. I did not see him flee. This is what others told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, you noted when you went into a building at one point in this time-frame that you went into this building and you saw that a shell had hit and you actually saw a dead body on the ground. Do you recall that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that that took place on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Back in 1997 you in fact noted that that took place on the morning of the 5th. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That 1997 statement is -- has got some inconsistencies which I have tried to correct. That is the one that I received, I beg your pardon, gave in 1997 by dictation and it was signed 1999. I fully admit I was not as attentive as I should have been in reviewing the two-year old transcript for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in fact, you did say in that 1997 statement that this took place at the government house, this event took place at the government house on the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And once again, sir, that is inaccurate. It took place on the evening of the 4th. And it was at what I call the ARSK headquarters which is not the Ministry of Defence and it is not the government house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you gave the statement in 1997, you had the location wrong and the date wrong?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Totally superfluous question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, the body that you saw, was it bodies or body?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Single.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again in 1997 you said it was several dead bodies in the lobby and I'm referring to the 1997 statement of 00884727?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I admit that that statement was not edited as I should have. I apologise. I saw one dead person dressed in some semblance of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us move on and the 5th was the day of your hospital visit. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted when I asked you for an individual that could verify this you gave me the same of a Sergeant Marcotte. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you said that he got a medal for his work at the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me put on the screen 1D170426. Blow that up a bit. Can you read that General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the Sergeant Marcotte that you were talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it doesn't say anything in that citation about receiving a medal about going to the hospital on the 5th of August, does it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact it says that he got a medal for going to get some -- retrieve some Kenyans who were located in the area of hostilities and transport them out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Might I be allowed to explain, subject to your concurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote up Sergeant Marcotte's recommendation for that specific act, and it was approximately two pages in length. It was in English and it was submitted to his home battalion, battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment. Almost 18 months went by and in those days the responsibility of the author the originator was to write up the citation and then other personnel would come up with the actual words that were to be used on the allocation or on the scroll that's presented. I was with the Sergeant when he was awarded. The first time we actually saw that section of words was when it was read aloud and there's a similar inconsistency in the meritorious decoration that I have. We approached our chain of command through an officer called Lieutenant-General Roi [phoen], who was deputy chief of Defence staff and we were told it is close enough. Sergeant Marcotte was not involved at all with the Kenyans. Sector South and Knin was not being bombed, and he was not involved in transported wounded Kenyan soldiers, he was involved in transporting wounded Serbian civilians. I'm very sorry to have taken so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you did tell us yesterday and this at page 210, 2010, when I asked you at line 20: "General do you know the name of anyone who was with you? Answer: Yes, actually now I do, Sergeant Marcotte, who was the Canadian Sergeant accompanied me on the trip and for that specific sequence of events he was awards the meritorious service medal?"

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And sir that is it accurate and truthful. He did accompany me. I can't - once again may I elaborate or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the name or names of anybody who may have seen me leave the compound inside an armoured vehicle which has no windows, though it's logical to assume there must be some folk who saw us return, speaking specifically of the incident you've raised on it's 5th of August, because we unloaded approximately 26 wounded Serbs in the middle of the compound. The vehicles were assembled down by the front gate so that is perhaps why we were out of sight, out of mind. But I am absolutely confident that if you can continue your investigations you will be able to find individuals that saw us do those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you said if we research the back documents on Sergeant Marcotte we will find no mention of him rescuing Kenyans?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, his narrative here, I think I've already explained, the background documents which I submitted, which I submitted to his battalion may not be the ones that actually got up to Government House. I have no control over that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe before we continue, could you tell me exactly where I find that there were Kenyans that were in this meritorious service decorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we move down, Judge, you start the second sentence -- actually it's the second sentence, which is somewhat long. Says on August 5th while the Croatian forces engaged in an attack against the city of Knin which was becoming bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I see the reference to Kenyan battalion area of hostilities, but not about Kenyans being -- because the witness said something about not Kenyans, Serb civilians, whatever, but in this document and it is not for the second time that you make that part of your question, I did not see anyone but I look at it now for the first time I see -- I do not see that it were Kenyans that were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was referring to the Kenyan area of responsibility. Thinking that is was the Kenyans that they were picking up, UN personnel, it's going into five members of the section and that was the deduction I came to. My point is at that this was contrary to what the General said yesterday as to what he got a medal for and who he was with. But I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stay with just this particular incident. I mean, you testified for us that you brought patients to the UN?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Most of them were -- hmm. Most of them were in no state to identify their profession. The ambulatory ones, no. To the best of my recollection and it has been a long time, I don't believe any of the ambulatory patients were soldiers. Some of those who were unconscious might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I mean those individuals that might have been you were taking them from a hospital and bringing them to the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why were you doing that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been approached that morning by a Serbian doctor who worked at the hospital, and he had indicated that there was no power, there was no light, no supplies, and essentially that the staff had left, and he and a male nurse were those that remained. He had left the male nurse at the hospital. He came to our compound to ask for assistance. As the attending physician to move his patients to Sector South military facilities and the area commander made the decision to -- to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it within the UN mandate to move soldiers in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have not actually stated that these personnel were soldiers. Have I said that I don't know if any were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is, is it within the UN mandate to move soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly within our mandate to move UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The -- when you were working for the UN, in Sector South, was it within your mandate to move either HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Leslie, I think the previous question was clear. Mr. Kehoe was clearly referring to the moving soldiers, not UN personnel. And I think you understood that. And you gave an answer which was fully correct, but ignored what the gist of the question was. Would you please carefully listen to the questions an answer them. Please proceed Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not within the mandate to move soldiers from any of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned likewise on the 5th that there was an event that took place at the gate of the UN compound where you were trying to get out with other UN personnel and you were stopped by HV soldiers who had come into the town. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let us go bring up 1D170374. There is again a video Your Honour. We have provided the booth with transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, has the document which is still on my screen at least already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No I will turned it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit D125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D125 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "LESLIE: Tell him that I'm Colonel Leslie and the Chief of Staff of Sector South, okay? "TRANSLATOR: Yes, I told him, but I'm trying to explain who you are. "LESLIE: Okay, good. We would like to freedom of movement to go through the city to make sure there is no ethnic cleansing." "TRANSLATOR: Well now there is some smaller actions. "LESLIE: Not a problem. Tell him we're professional soldiers and we accept the risk. We'd like to go now. "TRANSLATOR: Yeah, but I want to finish, please. "LESLIE: No, no, it's okay. "TRANSLATOR: And also we cannot take that risk that one of UN soldiers would be hurt. "LESLIE: We've already had several UN soldiers hurt. And I believe it's very important that we get out there to ensure that everything is being done according to the laws of war. If he objects to that then perhaps we have some serious problems. "TRANSLATOR: We don't want to take that risk because one of UN soldiers can be hurt from the other side, other soldiers -- and also they could said that it was made by [Indiscernible] soldiers. "LESLIE: Tell the Colonel thank you for his concern. Tell him the international community and the media are very interested in what's going on in Knin right now. We are getting on average 15 to 20 calls every ten minutes from CNN, Reuters, IPA, ITA, and unfortunately we have to tell them that we are blockaded here in the camp and we have no idea what the Croatian army is doing with the civilian population in the camp. "TRANSLATOR: [Indiscernible] "LESLIE: Good, please. We're not asking -- we're here to -- I beg your pardon -- "TRANSLATOR: But he already said, we don't like to take that risk because UN soldiers might be hurt of the other side" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, if I may, I'm sorry. Now, General, this video, there is some -- did you see some difference between what you were saying and what was being translated to the Croatian officer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minor nuances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At one point in the interview, I believe and I'll paraphrase what you were saying and we can go back and check, that you want to go out and make sure that the Croatian army is complying with the laws of war, and it is translated back to him that you want to go out and see for yourself. Did you see that discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sir, I take your word for it, but no I did not note it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during the course of this, there is an discussion where he is talking about enemy shelling on the 5th of August, and not wanting any UNCRO soldiers wounded. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was in fact ARSK shelling in the afternoon of the 5th of August, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fired into Knin.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. You are certainly can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I have a problem with the previous compound question and what it is that the witness was actually recalling and that is whether it was the desire not to have -- the expressed desire not to have UNCRO soldiers wounded or references to enemy shelling on the 5th of August and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can go back and play it and stop it. So if we go back to the beginning and I'll just stop it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "LESLIE: Tell him that I'm Colonel Leslie and the Chief of Staff of Sector South, okay. "THE INTERPRETER: Yes, I told him, but I'm trying to explain to you who is he. "LESLIE: Okay, good. We would like to freedom of movement to go through the city to make sure there is no ethnic cleansing." "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] it says that he is asking that he would like you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what she translates, General, is he is asking he would like you to allow him freedom of movement. Now there is nothing in that translation that says anything about ethnic cleansing, is there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we are talking about different levels of translation. We hear the words spoken. They are apparently translated by a -- by an interpreter, where I do not know, because that's then translated back again into English, and if there's any inaccurate translation, then, on the basis of what -- of your questioning at this moment of Mr. Leslie, I cannot identify where the problem is, whether it's the translation -- the interpreter who translate wrongly on that it is translated back into English not accurately. That is a puzzle for me, just for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do understand, Judge, I do think that I will tell you as an officer of the court our staff has been over this at some length and the difficulty in the translation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are specifically the kind of things I would appreciate if the parties could agree on that. It is just a technical issue. We don't have to spend time on it in court. If you play it and say here's a joint statement by Defence and Prosecution saying in this and this respect what is said is not an accurate translation. Then it takes you 15 seconds to deal with it. Parties can agree on it, it is one of the beautiful areas where there should be no dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can continue on, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] so that can he see what is going on in this city. If possible, we would like to move our vehicles out. I must tell you that due to activity there is still shooting going in the vicinity that is still dangerous for the time being and we need to wait for an additional period of time. "LESLIE: Not a problem, tell him we're professional soldiers and we accept that risk, we would like to go now. "TRANSLATOR: Yeah, but I want to finish, please. "LESLIE: No, not it's okay. "TRANSLATOR: He says that he understands, he is a professional soldier and he is prepared to take the risk. The Croatian army cannot take the risk and cannot allow for a single member of UNPROFOR, UNCRO become a casualty in the area. "Translator: But we can't take that risk and also we cannot take that risk that one of the UN soldiers be hurt. "LESLIE: We've already had several UN soldiers hurt. "TRANSLATOR: But we already had a several of UN soldiers hurt. "LESLIE: -- we've already had several UN soldiers hurt. "TRANSLATOR: But we've already had several UN soldiers hurt. "LESLIE: -- out there to ensure that everything is being done according to the laws of war. "TRANSLATOR: The most important thing would be for us to go out and see what's going on so as to be able to convince ourselves of what is going on."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, if I may, the comment that you made on the laws of war and we will clarify this but from the translation that we have it doesn't appear that that translator translated exactly what you said, does it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "LESLIE: -- we have some serious problems. "TRANSLATOR: He says if you object to that then we will assume that there are more serious problems. I already said that we do not want to take any responsibility for a single wounded UNPROFOR member who may be wounded by the enemy fire. "I apologise, and then this could be attributed to the members of the Croatian army. "LESLIE: Tell the Colonel thank you for his concern. "TRANSLATOR: Thank you for your concern. This is it the least of our ... "LESLIE: -- international community and the media are have interested in what is going on. "TRANSLATOR: All the world media are interested in the situation here. "LESLIE: -- 15 to 20 calls every ten minutes from the CNN-- "TRANSLATOR: They say that between to 15 to 19 calls from all over the world about what is going on and unfortunately they cannot tell them, we have to tell them that we are blocked. And we don't know what the Croatian army is doing at the moment what is going on in the streets. We are in constant contact with our superior command. I have not finished. I have not finished. He hasn't finished. As soon as our superior command concludes that this area is safe for UNCRO members and that they cannot be wounded by the enemy shells then they will certainly be given freedom of movement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In that second review General on some very key areas that you were interested in it does appear that there was a lack of communication, doesn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of UNCRO soldiers being wounded, I was asking you a question about in fact do you recall if there was shelling coming into Knin by the RSK in the afternoon of the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall such shelling having occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could put -- I will tender this exhibit, Your Honour, at this time, the video that we just played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to receive a -- a joint statement by the parties on what kind of mistakes there are in the translation, whether this is all -- if there is any dispute about what has been said or how it was translated then the Chamber will receive that information as well. And I add to that there was a certain portion in this -- in this video-clip, I think it was translated not exactly the same way by our interpreters and -- compared to how it was translated on the screen by the television, I take it the BBC, that was where difference was between I assume or I presume, that there will be major problems. Now it was unclear to me whether that was a reference to major problems caused by not allowing free movement or it was a suggestion or a reference that the denial of free movements would be an indicator that there would be major problems. That is not clear to me at this moment. If the parties got agree on how to understand this, there would also be appreciated by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will take your direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Registrar you were about to assign a number to this video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This goes in as D126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to D89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I note my words are not always very important but admission is important and it does not appear on the transcript. So D126 is admitted into evidence and I do not envy the job of our transcribers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can -- if I can turn to page 4 of that document, Mr. Monkhouse. And I would like the third beginning at about 051500?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I would like you to look at that insert for 05 -- by the way before we do this what time of day was this conversation that you had with the folks in front of the gate, if you know, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I can't recall. It was not the first conversation with the HV representatives because it took a while for the colonel to show up. So I'm sorry, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If we can just address ourselves to this insert that notes at about 05 at 1500 ARSK soldiers of unknown strength were seen occupying defensive positions in the general area of Strmica and gives the grid reference tanks and mortaring were seen in the same positions at 051815 they fired 12 rounds of artillery from Strmica towards Knin. Now, General, were you aware that there were reports coming into UN headquarters Sector South that the ARSK was firing in the afternoon of the 5th into Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if there's -- if Mr. Kehoe is aware of additional reports, I think they should be put to the witness or not included in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I'm asking this is an instances, I suspect that given a fact that a war was taking place that this was not the only incident and I am -- with this particular item in mind, I was -- I'm asking the General, just generally was he aware if there was any shelling coming from the RSK into Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asking about reports, I think, and not about -- but let's not -- if we would discuss it at this moment it would certainly not serve the interests of hearing evidence in the most efficient way. I will make an observation about it at a later moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, was not aware of reports that fire was being directed towards Knin and I note in this document it does say towards and not into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If I can just ask you one other question from that -- that video that we looked at, D126. You said that you had -- were getting 10 to 15 calls from the press and then mentioned, I think CNN Reuters, I believe you mentioned a few other news outlets. Were you the one talking to them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the main it was Mr. Alan Roberts and he had a variety of assistants, so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you take to any of them, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I did, because Mr. Roberts was very energetic in ensuring that appropriate coverage was given. I did my share, as did General Foran, as did Colonel Tymchuk [phoen], as did others. So, I'm sorry, I took a long time, yes, I did talk --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned during your direct examination the incident about the tank in front of the headquarters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry Your Honour, I don't have any recollection of that I would like to see a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, did you mention that during the course of your testimony that there was a tank parked out in front of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what the witness testified yesterday can be found in the transcript, yes? So don't ask the witness what he testified yesterday where we have reliable sources to establish this and if you give me one or two words, then I will look it up for you so that we know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did a tank park itself in front of your gate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was there a resolution of that difficulty or the tank being parked there relatively quickly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the tank remained there for several hours. I do not know the exact time at which it left because I was not at the gate when it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Captain Hill defused that situation relatively quickly, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Hill did exemplary work throughout his tour. I'm not aware of the specific incident that you're refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me talk about this particular video then, if I can bring this up as 1D170385.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, before we begin, that is Captain Hill, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... refugees. I got off the camp, I got down to the gas station, and what we ran into was the start line for them to do their final drive on Knin. So they said go back go, go back, I said okay. They had tanks, we didn't. One of the guys want the Colonel Leslie's pistol, Colonel said no. Then he wanted mine. For some reason, they want the Brownings. So he said well I will send my tanks to take them from the camp. So we laughed. So as I went back, he brought the APCs back and he had taken a T-54 and put it right in the gate with the barrel, like, right over the gate. And I came back and I said what are you doing? And he said I'm taking all your pistols. So we started killing ourselves laughing. I said, no, no you can't take the pistols, and I said, please move your tank. So they moved their tank and put it in the hold down, and after that he didn't ask for any more pistols."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General I notice you laughing, is that pretty much how that issue was resolved?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't actually aware of them -- that was the -- I wasn't aware that that issue of the pistols at the gate had come up. But as far as I know, I think that is how it was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will move this video in evidence and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D127 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D127 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, it was on page 1971 line 19. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I wasn't entirely off the mark I thought it was in there when I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you were in the compound on the 6th and were you not sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on the 6th, did you continue to inform Zagreb and -- did you continue to inform Zagreb about what had happened or what you believe had happened in Knin on the 4th and the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure we did I have no recollection of any specifics on the 6th my main focus was on trying to help the team bring a degree of coherence and stability to the displaced persons we had inside our compound. So I myself was not -- was not intimately involved in what was being head to UNCRO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you continue to talk to the media on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you -- in your conversation with the media tell them that you believed that there were 3.000 shells had landed and that you believed -- as a result of the shelling, likewise that there were 300 houses damaged and that there were 300 to 500 deaths. Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot recall the specifics of what I may have mentioned on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You knew, sir, that the information that you were providing to media sources whatever it was going to be published to the international community, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, were you aware, based on the information coming out of Sector South, that high-level meetings within the UN were taking place concerning that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn that at any point, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I do something to refresh your recollection, and that would be if we turn to D62. Now, D62 is a reference to a meeting that took place in Geneva and the summary notes that Spanish foreign minister Solana EU foreign affairs commission van den Broek, Carl Bildt and I met with Croatian foreign minister Granic for two hours on Sunday morning in Geneva to discuss the situations in Croatian and Bosnia. If we can go up a little bit there, Mr. Monkhouse. I'm sorry. Yes, foreign minister Solana's rebuke: "Foreign minister Solana crisply reiterated the EU position deprecating Croatian's military actions even as it was engaged in talks, condemning the shelling of civilian areas in Knin expressed concern over the humanitarian situation, protested about the treatment of UN troops and handed over a formal protest from Denmark about the treatment of its troops." If we can scroll up just a bit: "On humanitarian and UN related issues. Granic was pressed to explain the shelling of civilian areas in Knin and was told in no uncertain terms that that involved war crimes a matter falling within the province of the international tribunal in The Hague." Now, General, did you ever learn about these particular talks when you got back up to Zagreb into UNCRO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I -- not these particular talks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do know there were issues diplomatically as a result of the information that was being provided to the international community from Sector South. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the way I interpret the document you presented to me. Diplomatic and international issues were as a result of Croatian hostilities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask you a question. Is there any dispute as far as the Prosecution is concerned that reporting from this witness and -- as a Chief of Staff up in the hierarchy that the information would find its way into political meetings at a higher level; that's the first question. And the second question, is it in dispute that one could expect that if you give an interview to the international press that the information you reveal during such an interview would normally be published.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far as I understand both questions answer is there isn't any dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not any dispute. Then Mr. Kehoe if there are any specific matters to be addressed then of course we would like to hear. Would there have been, Mr. Tieger, any problem in tendering this document we have now in front of us? It is it in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is it in evidence already, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so therefore the information is available to the Chamber. Mr. Kehoe, we have spent quite a lot of time on -- on matters where I'm sometimes asking myself whether the questions are superfluous or whether these are facts, notorious facts. The questions whether in those circumstances you give an interview whether that would be published I still am in doubt whether it is superfluous or a notorious fact. If you disagree with that, at a later moment if it doesn't take too much court time you can make further submission on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I continue through I think that there is some building here that I have to ask the Court to bear with it. I understand Your Honours' concern but I think I will be getting through there relatively quickly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how quickly it goes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning our attention to the 7th you noted for us that you left on the 7th. And you noted for us that you testified that a Marine Lukovic drove you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who else was with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anybody else being with us. There may well have been, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were in the same car with Marine Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you drove this ten-hour drive back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think what happened was -- I beg your pardon, we changed to a different vehicle. The good marine captain and I knew each other and we had -- we had chats as we went to what was formally the zone of separation and from there a UN vehicle took me to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you aware that a Corporal Hatch and a Master Sergeant Parmley [phoen] stated that they drove you to -- Corporal Hatch said that he and Parmley drove you to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me, Master Bombadier Parmley was my driver, and he followed in the vehicle behind, but I don't believe he or Hatch were in the vehicle with the good marine captain and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was all the way -- and did Lukovic go with you all the way to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did he go to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to the zone of separation which was essentially the road down towards Split. And as soon as we got to the other side out of what was now -- well, formally the Croatian side of the zone of separation he went on his way, and Master Bombadier Parmley and the good sergeant took me to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you know that UN representatives and Mr. Akashi and others came to Knin on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you likewise know, or do you know, that a Mr. Flynn testified here several days ago, on the 11th of April, on page 1302, when asked about the damage in Knin on line 6 was asked: "When you arrived in Knin on the 7th is it fair to say you were surprised by the lack of damage to the town? Answer: I was surprised that there was less damage than I expected, yes. There certainly was damage but it did not seem to be extensive." Now, when you got to Zagreb, you -- is it true that you began to receive information from members of the international community that when they reviewed the damage in Knin it was not as extensive and as bad as had been reported by UN personnel before that date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I was not following the transcript at a certain moment where I see an urgent request from the court reporter to kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have attempted to and I get a message from time to time from my colleagues to do so, and I apologise to the booths and to the Chamber and to you, General, if I speak a little bit too quickly. I will do my best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the transcriber crying out for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I shouldn't forget the transcriber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were getting information that the reports where the damage was not as extensive as UN personnel had reported?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that likewise was being published in the media, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I can see no reason why it wouldn't be. I can't recall myself any specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall various media sources saying in terms that, that the damage in Knin was nowhere near as bad as had been reported by the UN prior to the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that when President Tudjman visited Knin, I believe, on the 7th, or the 6th, he had a media entourage with him who based on what they could see were transmitting a variety of messages, but as of sort of the afternoon of the 7th, I was en route and I was out of the information loop until probably the 9th or 10th. So does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, when you got to Zagreb, you were getting these reports both from members of the UN that were in Knin as well as media reports that the damage in Knin was not as extensive was as reported by UN Sector South headquarters when they were reporting on the 4th and the 5th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly some reports that were circulating that had different levels of damage ascribed to them. I don't remember any specific details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn our attention to D66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, when we are waiting to get this on the screen, it is not perfectly clear to me at this moment, is there an issue about whether these media reports existed? It appears to me a matter which is relatively simple to establish, and if there are -- I take it that they are copied or is the issue is whether this witness is aware of the media reports. If that is the issue, then why not just put to him as a fact which he can agree, I take it with Mr. Tieger, that they did exist. If that would be effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No I agree Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then just -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm actually interested in the particular reports. I didn't want to jump up too often or guide any answers in any way by any objection, but I'd like to know if the media reports referred to or UN reports referred to what damage they reported whether it was a discrepancies between reports, discrepancies between expectations built on other things. I think it is helpful to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond to that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are I think six, maybe eight various media articles which are published and cited in our pre-trial brief. And certainly we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're not in evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No they're not. But, Your Honour, I was asking my question is was he aware that that was happening and that is the significant point. I mean it is one thing to publish them but I was asking the General if he was aware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us turn our attention to the document that's on the screen and that is D66, if we can move down to downtown Knin. This is a cable from the United States government dated 14 August 1995. And it notes in the first sentence: "Although Knin was reportedly heavily shelled in the early hours of the hostilities few downtown buildings and residential areas showed signs of shell damage." Now, General, in that synopsis of that sentence is that basically the information you were getting back from not only representative coming from the United States but from other UN representatives concerning the level of damage in Knin when they had a chance to go through it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there were conflicting opinions and description on the level of damage in Knin. Some of those that you have alluded to or that have you identified describe the damage as very moderate and others less so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you began working in UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb on the 8th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually thought it was the 9th. But -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let just clear this up, sir, and it will be 65 ter 2749.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not moving that other exhibit into evidence because it is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it helps those who will read there transcript at a later date if you are referring to the D or P number, which gives a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D66 number that I just talked about on the screen, the US cable. It's in evidence. The item I have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is dated 8 August 1995 at 1300 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I stand corrected. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, I know it is difficult time-wise I'm just trying to clarify some times. And on this particular cable you were the drafter and the releaser, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we move down to the last paragraph here, you note, sir, that on line 3: "It is very important to sector headquarters gather immediate data and documentation of the time, place, nature of the alleged violation and who other -- who other witnesses were and, if possible, the units and personnel committing the violation?" Now, this, General, is a reference to what happened in Knin on the 4th and the 5th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, in part it was also a reference to what happened in all the sectors that UNCRO headquarters was responsible for not only Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you have a specific order to send this -- this document out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who gave that you order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Rodin [phoen], Al Rodin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did he give that to you orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, General, I didn't mean to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. As a Chief of Staff, the only freedoms I enjoy are the those which are signed by my commander, and in this case General Al Rodin was my new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D128 is admitted in into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, it is approximately time for a break, but I would first like to advise Madam Usher to escort Mr. Leslie out of the courtroom. We will have a break for approximately 25 minutes, Mr. Leslie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, how much time you think you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will probably take the balance of the day. I do understand and I don't want to speak for my colleagues, but I did discuss certainly with Mr. Kay and I don't believe at this point he intends on conducting any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, nothing arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Markac Defence. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not plan on any cross at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let see whether we can finish today with the cross-examination. We will then, I don't know, Mr. Tieger, whether you have at this moment already any intention to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, not I -- hopefully not at great length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore there is a fair chance that we might not finish the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think I will finish today on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well I can tell you, Mr. Kehoe, that there is some disagreement among the members of this Chamber. The disagreement is about whether you could have achieved what you do in cross-examination in 60 or in 50 per cent of the time you are actually using. So, you see, the Chamber is not fully in agreement. Could you please try to do it as efficiently as possible and as quickly as possible. We will have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We're moving off the document that is on the screen, which I believe was received as ... that has been received in evidence, the 8th of August, memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you testified, General, that you wrote your memo P84 on the 12th of August, the memo that we talked about during the Prosecutor's case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was my original suspected war crimes allegation given to the G2 of UNCRO. Is that the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the one?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, that several days later, you were -- were you aware that the UNMO teams in Zagreb were tasked to do an assessment of the damage caused by Operation Storm in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me bring up on the screen, P64. And just going through the first two paragraphs, paragraph 1 and paragraph 2. Notes UN team Pogonje [phoen] has made a provisional assessment of the damages caused by HV OPs 0406 August 95 in the town of Knin. The report is based on a run of 70 percent of Knin town and gives only a brief overview of the situation. In general, shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damages caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrated to the close vicinity of military objectives only few three to five impacts is observed in other urban areas. General, did you receive this in Zagreb while you were the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I did. This report was -- caused quite a bit of controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is called a provisional assessment but you were aware that a final assessment was provided to headquarters in Zagreb approximately a week later and that the final report was consistent with the provisional assessment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir I don't have that recollection. If could I see the report you are referring, to I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, I mean, nobody seems to be able to find that, General. I will tell you that. Neither the Office of the Prosecutor or anyone of the UN. But have you -- I can just tell you that, I don't know there is any source of dispute about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, nobody seems to be able to find that is a comment on the testimony of the witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not on this witness, Judge. What I'm saying is that I think there is an agreement that no one can locate that final assessment that Mr. Hernes [phoen] says was filed. I don't think that there is any disagreement between the Defence and the Prosecution on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a the bit confused by the question and answer as reflected in the transcript. Let me re-read it and see where the answer actually starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, I was trying not to mislead the general with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. But on the transcript I cannot see where the questions stops and where the answer starts. The witness says when asked whether the later report was consistent with the provisional assessment and then witness says that I don't seem to have that recollection that appears, seams to be the beginning of the answer, which does not appear on the transcript and then it says if -- could I see the report you are referring to, I would be very grateful. And then you say: I mean nobody seems to be able to -- or to find that. Yes. The word to find has two different meanings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Locate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now it is clear to me where I misunderstood the word to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Locate, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because whether it was consistent or not and if you say no one is able to find that that is to have any doubt as to the consistency that's what confused me but it is perfectly clear now you meant the word find in a literally way. I'm sorry for the time it takes me to understand the matter. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the issue a bit further. It is correct that -- well, the suggestion that there is an consensus that no one has been able to find the report suggests a consensus that such a report existed and that is of course a subject of controversy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just mistaken by a finding, relating that to the consistency or the inconsistency and that was just misunderstood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you know Colonel Hernes, who was the senior military observer in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And have you been advised that Colonel Hernes has told the Office of the Prosecutor that the final assessment was consistent with the findings of the provisional assessment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You did in fact, I think you said during the course of questions a few minutes ago, did in fact receive the information that was in the provisional assessment while you were in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall receiving this specific report but the contents and the contention that the shelling in Knin was as described in this report in grosso modo terms, yes, I received that as -- or more importantly so did my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General did your commander or did you do any other assessment, a UN assessment after you received that report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to remind you at this time I was Chief of Staff UNCRO working for General Al Rodin. UNCRO, to my knowledge, did not conduct any further assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned earlier, and this was at page 79, line 25, you said, "As a Chief of Staff the only freedoms that I enjoy are those granted to me by my commander." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- yes, that is accurate. For almost all professional militaries that is an accurate assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you, in -- after you received this provisional assessment, called down to officers that worked for you in Sector South, specifically Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk and Captain Berakov [phoen] and asked them to do him a favour and go out and look for evidence of indiscriminate shelling, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The general content is okay but I think this embraces an assertion that he received a provisional assessment. I believe the witness said he didn't actually receive the provisional assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You, General, noted for us that you understood that information had come back from Knin, from the UNMOs, that the -- there was no indiscriminate shelling in Knin. Was that basically information you got?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And after you received that information, you called down to Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk and Captain Berakov and asked them to go out and provide proof that the HV and HVO had committed war crimes by indiscriminately shelling the city. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall those exact words. May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure I'm sorry, I didn't mean to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut off your -- okay should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this issue of the low end assessment was received, or the information in it was promulgated via the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb for whom United Nations Military Observers actually worked because they weren't under General Al Rodin's command nor were they under General Foran's command. Discussions ensued between General Rodin, General Janvier, who was the commander UNPF. I was not present at these meetings. And on return General Rodin asked me to ask Sector South to either corroborate or amplify the information that was out there on the UNMO chain of command as a result of this activity. I don't recall the exact words that you ascribed to me as being those that I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we get to that General, and I don't have the exact words here, and I can get them, but didn't you just say that UNCRO earlier -- didn't you just say that UNCRO did not do any further assessments?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, and I apologise if I have been unclear, UNCRO was very small staff co-located with UNPF in Zagreb. We did not have any instruments with which to conduct any assessments. So in this case, Sector South personnel, Sector South was asked to do an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Sector South, sir, was part of UNCRO weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I was speaking of a Chief of Staff wherein my remit is for UNCRO headquarters. So if I misled you I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me put an item on the screen, 1D17-0211. And this I will tell you is an excerpt of the chronicle by Captain Berakov. We can blow up the bottom portion of that. 3 -- "31 August 1995. Up at 0630 hours. I attended morning prayers and went to Primostin. Colonel Leslie, now UNCRO COS, Chief of Staff, called Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk and asked him if I would be willing to do him a favour even though it was illegal, no photo-taking, and possibly dangerous. I didn't even have to think about it. I immediately said yes. "I was required to go into Knin and attempt to travel on every street possible. The purpose of the mission was to be able to find proof that HV, HVO had committed war crimes by indiscriminately shelling the city. MB, Master Bombadier, Parmley and I, found the evidence Colonel Leslie was looking for big time, more tomorrow." Did you do that General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall discussing with Colonel Tymchuk that Sector South do a damage assessment. Colonel Tymchuk was actually my opposite number, or the one I was most used to dealing with, in Sector South headquarters, as a senior operations officer. I do not know why the good captain would imply that this was illegal because no photos could be taken. The potential for danger was recognised. I do not recognise the exact words as described by the good captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you write an order or did you write a cable to anyone in Sector South telling them to conduct such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And -- you did?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you have any idea where that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I don't know. I don't know. But it was certainly something that sounds as if I would have done. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Chamber learn what it is, who the person is who drafted, even if there are no objections for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: His name is captain Phillip Berakov. And Phillip Berakov was a captain in Sector South headquarters. He is a Canadian -- he was a Canadian captain, since retired, and he was located in the Sector South headquarters, and I'm not certain when in the spring of 1995 but certainly I would say April to the fall of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, you confirm this? I mean of course we'd like to know what the origin of this document is. At the same time, of course, I'm asking Mr. Kehoe to give us that information, if that is undisputed we'll just accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. Under normal circumstances we would be introducing or seeking to review the document for a more fulsome submission, but this will in any event be part of Captain Berakov's 92 ter and the Prosecution will be submitting the entirety of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's good for to us know so that we have the full information about what the status this text is. Then, there are no objections? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
