utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D129, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D129 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to put on the ELMO, 1D170068. And the bottom paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is the citation that is on the web site for the governor general for Canada concerning your meritory service medal. And in the second sentence of this it says: "During intense artillery fire Lieutenant-Colonel Leslie organised and participated in several missions to rescue approximately 40 United Nations employees trapped in their residences and bring them to the United Nations camp, using armoured personnel carriers." General, you had told us during the course of your testimony yesterday that you were on one convoy with the Jordanians, where nothing of significance happened.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I would also add that in that one very short convoy my main role was that of guide. If there is any credit of rescuing those three civilians, it belongs to the Jordanian crew commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this particular citation -- and by the way while you were in that convoy, you said you didn't see anything?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing of significance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So where were the several missions that you participated in to rescue approximately 40 United Nations employees?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir -- I'll just wait. The citations for meritorious service, as mentioned, are just that. It's service which is of a meritorious nature and not specifically for bravery or courage. The citation is for my duties as Chief of Staff. I assume it was written by General Foran but I do not know. As mentioned when I was talking about the Sergeant Marcotte issue, his meritory service medal decoration was for a specific activity. Most of the reference in that which I actually wrote was for his trip to the hospital. The first time I became aware of this citation, and I was unaware that it was being prepared, was when it was at government house. The conclusion of this, I spoke to the vice chief of Defence staff and said, "I think you got to wrong. I think you're talking about 30 to 40 civilians from the hospital being moved to the UN compound." And after a bit of discussion he told me, "That's good enough. It's going to stay because you're going it for that, you're getting it for being the Chief of Staff duties." If you note, sir, I have never made any reference to any claim that I rescued Untied Nations civilian personnel. I take no credit or responsibility for those three folk. By the way, all credit goes to the Jordanian sergeants, the Sector South security officer, and Marine Dawes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, the government of Canada got the citation wrong in the Marcotte citation, and they got the citation wrong in your citation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more citations from that same batch, which have anomalies I'm not an expert on it because I don't know how they were actually written prior to being announced or awarded. I with speak with confidence on the Marcotte citation because I'm the one who wrote that. It had nothing to do with the Kenyans at least when I wrote it and nothing to do with rescuing personnel who were being bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I will offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D130 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Exhibit D130 is admitted into evidence. May I seek one clarification, Mr. Leslie, you said that you first saw it, I think you were talking about -- you said you assumed at that it was written by General Foran, and then you said something about you first knew about it at the government house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't find it immediately. What does that mean that it is printed and signed already what was the reference to that specific location? I take it, it is part of administrative procedure which I'm not a -- familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As is common practice, personnel do not write citation recommendations on themselves. That's written by their superiors and supervisors I became aware of this citation when it was actually being read aloud in a fairly large community with Sergeant Marcotte as well and immediately afterwards, as I mentioned, I spoke to the vice chief of the Defence staff of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean it was at the location where you were formally given this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Let's see, Mr. Kay, are matters as they were before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A few questions, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, General Leslie, a couple of question about two documents that were presented to you by the Defence. The first was the statement by Carl Bildt which referred to the and which was read to you that portion which was read to you referred to the shelling of the civilian population now being reported. First of all, based on what you observed on the 4th -- this is a document dated the 4th. Based on what you observed on the 4th of August in 1995 in Knin and the reports you have received concerning activity in other parts of the sector, was that information accurate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Secondly, the August 7th report from Mr. Stoltenberg to the Secretary-General that was referred to a few moments ago, in particular the portion on page 2, involving a discussion with Mr. Granic, in that report as pointed out to you by the Defence, Mr. Granic was pressed to explain the shelling of civilian areas in Knin. He said that most of the civilians had already fled the city before it was shelled. Based on your observations of the attack on Knin on the 4th of August, was that accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, based on my observations of the region of Knin, the city of Knin, his observation is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Granic also said there had been three military barracks in Knin. Did you observe that the shelling of Knin was directed at only the three military barracks in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked some questions about the concept of centre of gravity, and today as well, and also about air/land battle and you clarified that it was air/land battle 2000 and 2004. First of all, can you tell us and tell the Court, please, if there's anything about the concept of the centre of gravity that permits the shelling that you observed in Knin on August 4th. If that's not a clear question, let me ask it in a slightly different way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, my apologies. I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If -- I mean, that question was directed to your attention in connection with Knin. If Knin was a "centre of gravity," would that have permitted the shelling that you observed of Knin on August 4th and August 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does the concept of air/land battle that was brought to your attention permit the shelling that you observed of Knin on August 4th and August 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its totality, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What does that doctrine of air/land battle, what kind of shelling does it permit and how is that kind of shelling different from what you observed on August 4th and August 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of the battle space in air/land battle is one which is worthy of some discussion refinement if you wanted to apply that doctrine to the events that took place on the 4th and 5th of August I'm not aware of any battle space definition which includes civilian residences or infrastructure which are not being used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you have told the Court that the shelling that you observed reflected either a deliberate attempt to shell civilian structures and areas, or the indiscriminate shelling of such structures and areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now the Defence has asserted to previous witnesses that the shelling of Knin, and particularly -- or at least in part, if not particularly the shelling that took place in the centre part of Knin was not an indiscriminate attack but was directed at a certain number of particular military targets?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge, with all do respect I did not go through this on my direct examination. I mean -- if I understand the exploration of counsel I did not go through with this particular witness. So that was not part of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I say two things about that, maybe more. Number one, there is it an obligation in this institution of course to put the case to the witness. The Defence's case is being put to every other witness but not being put to this witness, who, indeed, seems to have a grater background and experience in just that area. Furthermore, this witness should have an opportunity, it seems to me, and this court should have the opportunity, to hear from this witness whether the alleged presence of military targets or certain military targets within or in the close vicinity of the residential areas he saw shelled is in any way in conflict with his assertion that the shelling was indiscriminate, and if not, why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, that should have been brought up on direct -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kehoe, calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This line of inquiry was not brought up on direct. There had to be a specific calculated decision by the Office of the Prosecutor not to do this. Now they want to go back into this on redirect examination? Well then just re-open re-cross on all of this. It's -- excuse me. It clearly was not a part of the direct examination and going into this on redirect is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court should be aware and the record will reflect that I attempted to do so on a couple of occasions. I thought then and think now the witness should be permitted to explain the -- what it is about the nature of the shelling that was, in his view, indiscriminate. I tried to do so. There were multiple objections to that and thereafter, in cross-examination, the area was skirted around, the suggestion was that somehow air/land battle made that appropriate and was in conflict with the witness's assertion that the shelling was indiscriminate. Same thing with the introduction of the provisional assessment. I mean, of course I'm in the Court's hands, but I would think that the Court would want to know this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there was an opportunity for the Prosecution to use General Leslie as an expert and file an expert report. That would have been proper. Now, General Leslie has a vast experience in artillery and as the Prosecutor well knew had the opportunity to do that, chose not to do it, chose not to introduce his five statements into evidence. They made a calculated decision about this. Then they came in on direct examination and tried to elevate him to some point as an expert without providing the expert testimony. Now what they can do, Your Honour, is they can take General Leslie off the stand and go back and get an expert report of some fashion. Which -- but that would mean we have other issues there because we're already this late into the case. But that was not -- this is was 13 years that this -- that General Leslie has been talking about this, five statements to the Prosecutor. And here we are, talking about targets after a specific decision by the Prosecution not to do it and not to qualify him as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, one question to start with. Isn't it true that the issue of potential military targets was introduced by the Defence as a couple of occasions to witnesses not being expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When -- when a particular witness was talking about a particular area, and if you recall, Judge, and then with regard to Mr. Dreyer, if you recall the caveat. The caveat was if Mr. Dreyer, these were military targets. And Your Honour stopped me and said, "Mr. Kehoe that's not established." I said, "I understand, Your Honour." If these are military targets, Mr. Dreyer, you were driving through them. Now, I understand the obligation at some point to do that, but that evidence was received with that caveat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber is not bound by any domestic rules of procedure and evidence. This Chamber also has the power to call upon the parties to present certain evidence. The matter is of a nature which the Chamber would like to receive information about, also from this witness. At the same time, one can wonder which party should then provide that information to this Chamber. The Chamber invites Mr. Tieger and Mr. Kehoe to see whether they come to agreement as who will elicit this evidence, if the witness has any knowledge about the matter, from this witness. If you do not agree on who will do it, and of course, if the one party puts questions in relation to the matter to the witness, the other party will have an opportunity to cross-examine, or at least to put questions to the witness as well. If you don't decide on who will do it the Chamber will do it. So you are invited to seek who will elicit this evidence from this witness, if he can give any evidence about it. The Chamber is not in this way applying Rule 90 (H). We are not in that area. The Chamber, on the basis of the arguments we just heard and on the basis of the evidence the Chamber received in relation to other witnesses is just interested to see whether this witness can tell us anything about it. Yes. Therefore, Mr. Tieger, at this moment, until you have had a conversation with Mr. Kehoe, please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say on this score, it was not part of the direct examination. So, clearly, there has not been a proofing statement provided to the conference on that score. And if in fact this is going to be elicited by the Prosecution, we would certainly ask for the proofing statement because I'm sure that he has discussed this with General Leslie prior to yesterday or certainly prior to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- I take it that, Mr. Tieger, if during proofing, anything has arisen in your conversations or conversations of the OTP with Mr. Leslie, which would not be favourable to your case but perhaps favourable to the other case, then I take it that you would have immediately disclosed such information to the Defence under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, if in the proofing anything would have arisen at any moment which you should have been aware about, Mr. Tieger was under a obligation disclose that to you. So, therefore, I take it that this could have been the first part of your conversation with Mr. Tieger but since you addressed the Chamber, I briefly addressed the matter as well. Mr. Tieger, you can continue at this moment but not on this subject until you have had a conversation with Mr. Kehoe and the Chamber will hear whether you agree on who is going to elicit this evidence. And again, I emphasise this is not examination/cross-examination. This is evidence the Chamber asks the party to present, and which party is, first of all, for you to agree upon; if not, the Chamber will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In that case, I think I'm ready to have that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Leslie, we are ten minutes before we usually adjourn for the day. You may have understood from the conversation that there might be a certain chapter to be dealt with by either Prosecution or Defence, not necessarily even you, Mr. Kehoe, I don't know whether any other candidates, I take it that you're the one who is most interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think I'm elected, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that we would like to continue tomorrow. I see no reasonable risk, no risk, that we would not finish by tomorrow, although it may take, I would suggest that it would take not more than half a session to elicit the evidence and then certainly not more than half a session to put questions to the witness. Yes Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's, I think, a bit optimistic, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Think about the 50 and the 60 per cent and see what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am thinking, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd like to instruct you again that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd liked to you back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands there was some uncertainty about what would happen on Friday. Mr. Leslie, his testimony will be concluded somewhere tomorrow morning. It entirely depends on the parties what will happen on Friday because if the next witness can be examined and cross-examined tomorrow, then I do understand that there is no other witness available for this week, Mr. Tieger, is that correct? That would also mean that we would not sit on Friday. If, however, we cannot conclude the testimony of the witness to be called tomorrow, I couldn't say the Chamber will continue on Friday. I'm not available this Friday, and the other Judges have informed me that they -- where they earlier considered to sit under Rule 15 bis, that they have decided to continue the examination hearing the evidence the next witness to be called on Friday so as to enable that witness to return home before the weekend. That's as far as Friday is concerned. Are there any other matters to be raised at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please inform Mr. Nilsson, our legal officer about any agreement or about any lack of agreement on who will elicit the evidence from Mr. Leslie tomorrow on the issue of, I would say, objects or facilities that one could consider as qualifying as legitimate targets. And of course the Chamber is, as before, mainly interested to know what did he include as his personal knowledge in his assessment of the situation, rather than to have a lengthy discussion on what a legitimate military target is, because, as the Chamber has decided before, finally it is the Chamber who will decide that, but the Chamber may consider observations in this respect by knowledgeable people, even if not called as experts. We earlier explained that sometimes what someone can observe or can know, can hear, needs some kind of an interpretation where this interpretation, the ability to interpret is not the same for every witness. We stand adjourned until the 24th of April, 9.00, this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
